Reproductive output in laboratory cultures of Eisenia andrei has been characterized in some detail. Under stable conditions of 22.5 °C [T = 22.5 °C], adults approach their maximum recorded body mass of 0.93 grams [Wwi = 0.93 grams], a size that appears to represent an asymptote beyond which further somatic growth is negligible. At this temperature, each worm produces approximately 2 to 3 cocoons per week [F_R_i = approximately 2 to 3 cocoons per week], and each of those cocoons yields, on average, roughly 2.7 neonates per cocoon [N_R_i = roughly 2.7 neonates per cocoon]. This level of reproduction reflects a high daily output for a compost-dwelling oligochaete and underpins the species’ rapid colonization of organic-rich substrates. The consistency of these figures under controlled thermal regimes suggests that key aspects of life-history scheduling, including both growth and gamete production, are tightly coupled to ambient temperature.

Neonatal life stages in Eisenia andrei are remarkably brief, a feature that accelerates its generational turnover relative to many larger-bodied lumbricids. At the standard culture temperature of 22.5 °C [T = 22.5 °C], the interval between oviposition and the hatching event spans approximately 21.7 days [ab = approximately 21.7 days]. The newly emerged worm, having exhausted its yolk reserves, weighs only 0.02 grams [Wwb = 0.02 grams], a value that underscores the extremely altricial nature of the clitellate hatchling. This minuscule starting mass imposes a steep challenge for early survival in the competitive environment of a vermicomposting bin, where juveniles must quickly locate microbial-rich substrates to fuel their imminent growth spurt. The short incubation period likely confers an advantage by reducing the window of vulnerability for the embryonated egg stage.

The progression from birth to the onset of reproductive competence in Eisenia andrei is compressed, reflecting its status as a classic r-selected invertebrate. At a constant 22.5 °C [T = 22.5 °C], individuals require 36 days after hatching [tp = 36 days after hatching] to reach puberty. By this stage, the worm has invested heavily in somatic tissue, achieving a wet weight at puberty of 0.772 grams [Wwp = 0.772 grams], which represents a substantial fraction of its ultimate adult mass. This rapid somatic development is metabolically expensive, and the high juvenile growth rate observed in this species likely depends on a continuously available supply of decomposing organic matter. The efficient conversion of ingested material into body mass is a hallmark of the species’ adaptation to ephemeral, nutrient-rich habitats.

Adult body size in Eisenia andrei is modest even by lumbricid standards, with the maximum total length recorded in well-fed individuals reaching just 13 centimeters [Li = 13 centimeters]. This relatively short body length, combined with a narrow diameter, facilitates movement through the interstices of compost and manure piles, the worm’s typical microhabitat. The ultimate wet weight of 0.93 grams [Wwi = 0.93 grams] appears to be a robust species-level trait, with little variation among geographically disparate populations maintained under similar feeding regimes. This consistent adult size likely reflects a ceiling imposed by the physical constraints of the burrowing environment and the respiratory demands of living in high-ammonia, low-oxygen substrates. Comparisons with the larger and deeper-burrowing Lumbricus terrestris reveal stark contrasts in both morphology and life-history tempo.

Longevity in Eisenia andrei has been extrapolated from related taxa, as direct long-term cohort studies remain limited. Available data, drawing on patterns observed in the deep-burrowing Lumbricus terrestris, suggest that the maximum lifespan under optimal laboratory conditions may approach 2601 days [am = 2601 days] when kept at 22.5 °C [T = 22.5 °C]. Such a protracted potential lifespan is remarkable for an animal with such rapid early growth and high fecundity, and it may reflect a bet-hedging strategy in which adults retain the capacity for reproduction over many consecutive seasons. Even after reaching sexual maturity at approximately 0.77 grams, individuals continue to allocate resources toward maintenance, allowing them to persist through periods of suboptimal food quality. This combination of high early fecundity and extended adult survival is a defining feature of the species’ life-history profile within the family Lumbricidae.
